# discoverHTE

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->

*discoverHTE* estimates what a continuous exposure does on average, and then asks whether
it does the same thing to everyone. The exposure-response function (ERF), also called a
causal dose-response curve, describes how the expected outcome changes as the exposure
moves across its range with the measured covariates held fixed. `estimate_erf()` estimates
it using the doubly robust estimator of Kennedy et al. (2017), and `rpart_erf()` then
searches a set of candidate effect modifiers for the subgroups whose ERFs differ most,
returning a tree in which each node carries its own dose-response curve.

Estimating the curve and partitioning on it are separate steps on purpose. The ERF is fit
once, with whatever nuisance models suit the data, and the tree is grown from that fit
without re-estimating anything, so the same curve can be partitioned several ways at
little cost.

## Installation

Install *discoverHTE* from GitHub:

``` r
pak::pak("fbargaglistoffi/discoverHTE")
```

## Estimating an exposure-response function

`estimate_erf()` takes a two-part formula: the outcome on the left, then the exposure and
the covariates separated by a `|`. Everything to the right of the `|` is adjusted for.
Here the exposure is the log of blood lead level among 2521 children, and the outcome is a
mathematics test score.

```{r example}
library(discoverHTE)

data("nhanes3lead", package = "adrftools")

erf <- estimate_erf(Math ~ logBLL | Age + Male + PIR + Smoke_in_Home + Race,
                    data = nhanes3lead)

erf
```

Plotting the result draws the curve, a simultaneous confidence band, and the distribution
of the exposure along the top.

```{r plot-erf, fig.alt = "Estimated exposure-response function for mathematics score against log blood lead level, falling steadily from about 8.7 to 6.2 points across the observed exposure range, with a simultaneous confidence band and a rug of the exposure distribution along the top."}
plot(erf)
```

The curve falls across the whole range, so a higher blood lead level is associated with a
lower score throughout rather than only above some threshold.

The `erf` component of the fitted object evaluates the curve wherever you ask and returns
the estimates with their covariance.

```{r evaluate}
est <- erf$erf(c(0, 3))

est$est
```

Moving from a log blood lead level of 0 to 3 is associated with a drop of about
`r round(diff(range(erf$erf(c(0, 3), vcov = FALSE)$est)), 1)` points on a test scored out
of 20.

How the two nuisance functionals are estimated is set by the `method` argument.
`method_glm()`, the default, uses generalized linear models. `method_superlearner()` stacks
several learners, `method_gamlss()` models the whole conditional distribution of each
variable, `method_bartisan()` uses Bayesian additive regression trees, and
`method_negbinomcens()` handles count outcomes with interval-censored cells.

## Finding subgroups whose curves differ

`rpart_erf()` takes the fitted ERF and a one-sided formula naming the candidate effect
modifiers. At each node it searches every candidate split and keeps the one whose two
subgroup ERFs differ most, measured by the `metric` argument.

```{r tree}
tr <- rpart_erf(erf, ~ Male + Race + PIR + Smoke_in_Home,
                max_depth = 3, min_samples = 100)

summary(tr)
```

Plotting the tree draws a panel at every internal node, each showing the ERFs of that
node's two children.

```{r plot-tree, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "The fitted tree, with a panel at each internal node showing the two child subgroup exposure-response curves overlaid, arranged in the shape of the tree."}
plot(tr)
```

Any single node can be lifted out with `[[` and plotted on its own, with its branch path
as the subtitle.

```{r plot-node, fig.alt = "Exposure-response function for the node containing children with a poverty-income ratio below 2.69, shown on its own with its branch path as the subtitle."}
plot(tr[[2]], density = FALSE)
```

The ERF is a confirmatory estimate, with influence-function standard errors that are
cluster-robust where clustering is supplied. A tree grown and evaluated on the same data
is not. It searches many candidate splits and keeps the best, so the bands at its nodes
do not pay for that search. `honest_erf_tree()` grows the tree on one half of the sample
and estimates the ERF at each of its nodes on the other half, so the bands at its nodes
are valid given the tree.

```{r honest}
set.seed(1234)
ht <- honest_erf_tree(Math ~ logBLL | Age + Male + PIR + Smoke_in_Home + Race,
                      data = nhanes3lead, modifiers = ~ Male + Race + PIR + Smoke_in_Home,
                      max_depth = 2, min_samples = 100)

summary(ht)
```

## Learn more

`vignette("discoverHTE")` covers the package's features in order, from bandwidth selection
and cross-fitting to derivative ERFs, the objective functions available for splitting, and
honest trees.
`vignette("negbinomcens")` illustrates the count model with simulated county-level
data, age-specific population denominators, and suppressed cells. For the application to
fine particulate matter and mortality, see [the methods paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30838).

## Reference

Kennedy, E. H., Ma, Z., McHugh, M. D., & Small, D. S. (2017). Non-parametric methods for
doubly robust estimation of continuous treatment effects. *Journal of the Royal
Statistical Society: Series B*, 79(4), 1229-1245.
<https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12212>
